55: “But what is this love that consecrates marriage?” said, suddenly, the voice of the nervous and taciturn gentleman, who, unnoticed by us, had approached.
44: The clerk listened and smiled, with the air of one accustomed to store in his memory all intelligent conversation that he hears, in order to make use of it afterwards.
42: “The main thing, and the thing which such people as he do not understand,” rejoined the lady, “is that only love consecrates marriage, and that the real marriage is that which is consecrated by love.”
39: “Yes, gentlemen,” said the lawyer, “we are still a long way from the European ideas upon marriage. First, the rights of woman, then free marriage, then divorce, as a question not yet solved.” . . .
37: [*] The Domostroy is a matrimonial code of the days of Ivan the Terrible.
35: “He is a Domostroy,”[*] said the lady. “What savage ideas about a woman and marriage!”
33: “There’s a little Old Testament father for you,” said the clerk.
31: Scarcely had the old man gone when a general conversation began.
29: “Oh, that’s another matter,” said the merchant, severely. “Good-by,” he added, rising. He wrapped himself in his cloak, lifted his cap, and, taking his bag, left the car.
27: “And you yourselves, at Kounavino, did you not lead a gay life with the pretty girls?” asked the lawyer with a smile.
25: “Yes, the feminine sex must be dominated in season, else all will perish.”
23: At that moment the conductor passed, asking for the tickets for the next station. The old man gave up his.
21: “He is an imbecile,” said the old man. “If from the first he had not allowed her to go in her own fashion, and had kept a firm hand upon her, she would be living honestly, no danger. Liberty must be taken away from the beginning. Do not trust yourself to your horse upon the highway. Do not trust yourself to your wife at home.”
19: Everybody was silent. The clerk moved, advanced, and, not wishing to lag behind the others in the conversation, began with his eternal smile:
17: “It happens among the upper classes, not among us,” answered the old man. “And if any husband is found who is such a fool as not to rule his wife, he will not have robbed her. But no scandal, nevertheless. Love or not, but do not disturb the household. Every husband can govern his wife. He has the necessary power. It is only the imbecile who does not succeed in doing so.”
14: “And if it does happen, all the same? You will admit that it does happen?”
13: “That should not happen,” said the old man. “He must have his eyes about him.”
11: “And if the wife deceives her husband, what is to be done?” said the lawyer.
9: “Oh, no, she will not be forced,” said the lady. “Where there is no love, one cannot be obliged to love in spite of herself.”
7: This unexpected argument pleased the clerk, and he uttered a murmur of approbation.
6: “If she does not love him!” repeated the old man, stormily, and knitting his brows; “why, she will be made to love him.”
4: “Yes, but you will admit, I think, that woman is a human being, and has feelings like her husband. What should she do if she does not love her husband?”
2: His tone of authority evidently subjugated his hearers. Even the lady felt crushed, but she did not surrender.
